summary_paragraph: The patient, a woman with HIV/AIDS (CD4 ~59, off antiretroviral therapy with prior PCP) and ESRD on hemodialysis (MWF) via tunneled catheter, was admitted for pleuritic substernal chest pain with odynophagia. Cardiac and pulmonary embolism/aortic syndrome evaluations were negative (EKG without ischemia, CK-MB flat with troponin elevation attributed to ESRD, CTA chest negative). GI evaluation including upper GI series and EGD showed mild gastritis and duodenitis, treated with omeprazole with symptom improvement; aluminum-containing antacids were avoided due to ESRD. During hospitalization she developed high fevers and blood cultures grew coagulase-negative staphylococcus consistent with catheter-associated bacteremia; she was treated with vancomycin (initially with cefepime until cultures clarified), and due to persistent fevers the infected dialysis line was removed with a brief line holiday. After unsuccessful neck access attempts due to central venous occlusions, a right femoral tunneled dialysis catheter was placed and dialysis resumed. Near discharge she had a transient retrocardiac opacity on chest X-ray treated briefly with cefepime; cultures remained negative and repeat imaging improved, so antibiotics were stopped. She restarted PCP/MAC prophylaxis (Bactrim and azithromycin), received renal supportive meds (sevelamer, cinacalcet, nephrocaps, folic acid, aspirin), and was discharged home with services with a plan to continue vancomycin dosed at dialysis for 10 additional days and to follow up for HIV care, dialysis access planning, and chronic pain/neurology care.
problems: Bloodstream infection due to central venous catheter (coagulase-negative staphylococcus bacteremia)
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV/AIDS) with low CD4 and history of PCP; off HAART with adherence barriers
End-stage renal disease on hemodialysis with difficult vascular access; temporary right femoral tunneled catheter
Chest pain with odynophagia (non-cardiac; improved with GI therapy)
Chronic pain syndrome/myalgias/arthralgias (managed with PRN opioid; outpatient neurology follow-up)
History of herpes zoster with postherpetic neuralgia (no active lesions during admission)
Transient retrocardiac opacity on chest X-ray treated briefly with antibiotics; resolved on repeat imaging
